newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Robotics aims to calm merger fears.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Robotics aims to calm merger fears.

text.p: U.S. Robotics Corp., which last week agreed to merge with 3Com Corp. in a $7.3 billion stock deal, used its annual meeting Wednesday to calm fears about the deal and urge shareholders to focus on the long term.
Casey Cowell, chairman and chief executive of the modem maker, set out to clear up what he called "misperceptions" about the deal.
"As I stand here before you today, I truly cannot think of a better business combination for everybody," Cowell told the audience of about 350 people.

Last week, U.S. Robotics and 3Com agreed to a merger in which U.S. Robotics shareholders would receive 1.75 3Com shares per U.S. Robotics share. Shares of U.S. Robotics closed lower the day after the announcement, with some industry analysts saying the per share price was too low.

Cowell explained that customers were looking for a one-stop shop for networking products, and said 3Com provides the Local Area Network technology that U.S. Robotics is missing. He said both companies have leading market shares in their core products.
"As shareholders of U.S. Robotics, you will have the opportunity to participate from the onset in what we believe will be the best networking company," Cowell said.

During a question and answer session held after Cowell's presentation, many shareholders praised the company for a strong year and for being first to market with its 56 kilobit per second modem technology, called x2.

"Going into it, I thought, 'What's the justification for why I want to stay a shareholder?'" James Rothschild, an account manager for Marshall Industries and a U.S. Robotics shareholder, said after the meeting.
He said he will keep his shares, adding that Cowell explained the merger very effectively. "It will create a powerhouse," Rothschild said.
In answer to a question, Cowell said the company's stock fell after the merger was announced because of "skittishness" in network industry stocks.

"Look at the power of the combination and the portion of the combination our side is getting. That's what I felt and the directors felt was very compelling," Cowell said in an interview following the meeting.
U.S. Robotics will own about 48 percent of the combined company.

Cowell said misperceptions in the investment community surrounding the deal included talk that the company was insecure about the x2 technology. He said the deal had even been called a desperation move by two weak companies.
"Nothing could be farther from the truth," Cowell said, adding that the initial response to the x2 technology has been very good.
Cowell said both companies carried out extensive due diligence and were confident in the merger.
3Com has seen its stock price plummet since the first of the year, after it warned that its fiscal third-quarter revenues would be weaker and said it cut prices on its key adapter card products.

"I can't comment on the due diligence process, but looking at their position in the marketplace and their technology ... I can tell you that we absolutely feel that this is the best combination in the history of our industry and will result in the greatest strength going forward," Cowell said.

He rebuffed claims that U.S. Robotics management was looking for a way to sell out. He said his new job as vice chairman of the combined company will be much like his current position -- to focus on vision and strategy.
Cowell said he will likely be the largest individual shareholder in the new 3Com. "If we had wanted to sell out, we would have pursued a cash transaction," he said.
U.S. Robotics closed up $2.625 at $60 and 3Com added $1.625 to end at $35.4375, both on Nasdaq.
